title: Analytical Theory for Anomalous Diffusion in the Anderson Model with Heavy Tails
authors: Elizaveta Safonova, Aleksey Lunkin, Mikhail Feigel'man
abstract: We develop an analytical theory of anomalous transport in a noninteracting Anderson model with heavy-tailed hopping amplitudes. The broad distribution of hopping amplitudes gives rise to an extended intermediate-time regime with a subdiffusive effective exponent, despite the absence of interactions or genuine many-body effects. By solving the transport equations analytically, we derive the time dependence of the mean-square displacement and identify a continuous crossover from an intermediate anomalous regime to asymptotically diffusive transport. As the localization transition is approached, the spatial extent of the subdiffusive window diverges parametrically, while the crossover to conventional diffusion remains finite in units of $Γ_0^{-1}$. This produces an increasingly broad anomalous transport regime in space that can closely resemble Griffiths-type transport observed near the many-body localization transition. Our results demonstrate that rare hopping processes alone provide a microscopic single-particle mechanism for robust transport anomalies, establishing an analytical benchmark for distinguishing interaction-induced effects from disorder-driven dynamics.
summary: This paper develops an analytical theory demonstrating that heavy-tailed hopping amplitudes in the noninteracting Anderson model cause robust subdiffusive transport over an intermediate time scale. By solving complex transport equations using advanced field-theoretic methods, the authors establish a single-particle mechanism for these anomalies, providing a critical tool to distinguish disorder effects from many-body interactions.
main_problem: The paper develops an analytical theory to understand anomalous transport (subdiffusion) in the Anderson model when hopping amplitudes are governed by heavy-tailed distributions.
main_result: It shows that rare hopping processes alone can induce a robust, intermediate subdiffusive regime, providing a single-particle mechanism distinct from interaction effects. This anomaly eventually crosses over to conventional diffusion at long times.
method: The analysis employs advanced theoretical techniques, including solving transport equations by mapping the problem onto the Lévy–Rosenzweig–Porter (LRP) matrix ensemble and utilizing supersymmetric field-theoretical formalisms.
model_or_system: The system is a noninteracting Anderson model on a lattice with diagonal disorder ($u_n$) and hopping amplitudes ($t_{nm}$) following heavy-tailed power laws. The Hamiltonian describes single-particle dynamics in the presence of strong, broad disorder.
key_observables: Mean-square displacement $\langle r^2(t) angle$, the effective subdiffusive exponent $\xi(t)$, and frequency-dependent conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$.
important_parameters: The tail exponent $\mu$ of the hopping amplitudes ($P_\mu(|t|) \propto |t|^{-\mu}$), which controls the transition between diffusive ($\mu=2$) and localized ($\mu 	o 1$) regimes.
main_assumptions: The theory relies on analytical solutions to transport equations, approximations like the saddle-point method in field theory, and assumes that the anomalous regime is a parametrically extended crossover rather than a true asymptotic phase.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scaling exponent $\xi(r)$ showing subdiffusion extending beyond the mean free path for small $\mu$, and compare calculated $\langle r^2(t) angle$ with numerical simulations, confirming preasymptotic enhancement over diffusion.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the model parameters (heavy tails, Anderson Hamiltonian), developing the mathematical framework using LRP ensembles or supersymmetric field theory, deriving expressions for correlation functions and conductivity, and finally analyzing the time/frequency dependence to characterize the crossover between anomalous subdiffusion and normal diffusion.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant because it provides a rigorous analytical benchmark for understanding transport anomalies in disordered quantum systems. The separation of disorder-driven effects from interaction-induced ones is crucial for interpreting experimental results in AMO physics, especially concerning localization transitions.
